source: backtest/06_chain.py over FDA's shortage history (31 archived snapshots, Oct 2022 to Oct 2026), DailyMed SPL plant lists, FDA's registration file and FDA Data Dashboard exports. Raw outputs: backtest/backtest_runs.txt.
question: When FDA posted a shortage, had FDA already acted against a plant named on the product's label in the two years before?
window: Shortages first posted as Current from 2022-01-01; signals in the 730 days before the posting
signalDefinition: At a plant whose label operations include MANUFACTURE, API MANUFACTURE or STERILIZE: an OAI inspection, a warning letter, an injunction, a seizure, or an import-alert listing (66-40 or 66-79). VAI inspections and recalls are counted separately.

cases.note: 92 of 138 recent shortages had at least one manufacturing plant we could place by FEI; the rest name no plant on the label, or a plant we cannot place.

strict.label: Dated by when it was public
strict.dating: An inspection counts from its classification letter (FMD-145), or 90 days after it closed when the letter date is missing.
strict.reading: No lift over products that never went short. Using only what FDA had published, a plant action is not a predictor.

endDated.label: Dated by when the inspection closed
endDated.dating: An inspection counts from the day it ended, when FDA handed the plant its Form 483. The OAI label itself came later, so this uses hindsight about which inspections became OAI.
endDated.reading: About twice as common among shortage products, and 3 times as common among injectables over one year (14.7% vs 4.7%), but with hindsight.

controls.note: 623 random prescription products whose NDC and generic name never appear in FDA's shortage history, each given a reference date drawn from the cases; 336 had a placeable manufacturing plant.

ppv.note: If the close-dated signal were used as an alarm: about 1 in 14 flagged injectables would go short within a year. Order of magnitude only (crude 5-year prevalence).

recalls.note: Class I/II recalls at the plant or labeler are common everywhere, so they carry little information on their own.

events.label: FDA inspection ends; later classified OAI

examples.note: The same plant is named on BluePoint's cisplatin label (shortage posted 2023-02-10) and on Accord's methotrexate tablets (posted 2023-07-21).
The shortage was posted 14 days after the first warning letter.
Before the 2022 study window; shown because the trail is complete.

events.label: FDA posts the IV fluid shortages

examples.note: The counter-example. The OAI is real, but the hurricane caused this shortage. A trail is not a cause, and Upstream says what FDA's records show without claiming why.

caveats: Look-ahead: plant lists come from today's labels and registration file, and import-alert lists show firms listed now.
FDA names one shortage several ways (four lidocaine names, three albuterol names), so episodes are not independent; a few plants (Intas Sanand, Hospira, Baxter, Nephron) recur.
Six variants of this test were run. We report the strictly dated one first and the close-dated one beside it; the p-values are optimistic for that reason.
FDA posted only 18 new shortage names from 2024 to 2026, so the window starts in 2022 and n is small.
API (active ingredient) plants are almost invisible on labels: 42 of 708 shortage labels name one.
About a third of labels name no plant at all; we fall back to label text or the application holder and say so.
conclusion: The public trail is often there and explains a shortage after the fact: in 1 in 8 recent shortages by strict dating, and 1 in 4 by close dating, FDA had acted against a named plant, typically about three months before the posting. It is not a forecast. Upstream is built to explain, cite and act on what is known, not to predict.
